analysis.one_liner: Extends and expands government health coverage for low-income children through 2012, paid for with higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House 265-142 and the Senate 64-30, but President Bush vetoed it on December 12, 2007, and the House fell 10 votes short of the two-thirds needed to override, 260-152.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have renewed the Children's Health Insurance Program through 2012 with much larger funding, covering millions of low-income children and pregnant women whose families earn too much for Medicaid but can't afford private insurance. States would get new options to enroll kids automatically, cover dental and mental health care, and cover pregnant women. The money would come from higher federal excise taxes on cigarettes and other tobacco products, plus a small one-quarter reduction in estimated tax payments for corporations with at least $1 billion in assets.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income children and pregnant women who are uninsured or at risk of losing coverage, and their families. States also benefit from performance bonuses and a contingency fund when enrollment runs higher than expected.

how_it_helps.text: Reauthorizes CHIP through FY2012 at increased funding levels, rising from $9.125 billion in 2008 to $13.75 billion in 2011, with a one-time $13.7 billion appropriation for the first half of 2012 [S3][S5].
States get new options to cover targeted low-income pregnant women under CHIP, with automatic enrollment for children born to women receiving pregnancy-related assistance [S3][S5].
Requires CHIP plans to cover dental services needed to prevent and treat oral disease and provides mental health parity with medical and surgical benefits [S3][S5].
Funds outreach and enrollment grants, a national enrollment campaign, and simplified eligibility verification so eligible children actually get enrolled [S3].
Amends the Family and Medical Leave Act to give family members of injured servicemembers up to 26 workweeks of leave in a 12-month period to care for them [S2][S5].
The bill states its purpose is to enroll all six million uninsured children who are eligible but not enrolled [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, through higher federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, smokeless tobacco, pipe tobacco, and roll-your-own tobacco, with a floor-stock tax due by April 1, 2008. Corporations with at least $1 billion in assets also receive a one-quarter reduction in their third-quarter 2012 estimated tax payment.

drawbacks.text: The tobacco tax increase falls on smokers, a group that includes many lower-income people, though tobacco use also drives public health costs [S2][S3].
The bill denies new federal CHIP payments for children in families with income above 300% of the poverty line, limiting what higher-cost states could do [S2][S3].

The bill lowers the third-quarter 2012 estimated tax payment for corporations with at least $1 billion in assets from 114.75% to 113.75% of the amount otherwise due — a small but unambiguous break for the largest corporations [S3][S5].
The bill bans new health opportunity account demonstration programs and phases out CHIP coverage of nonpregnant childless adults after 2008, removing coverage some states had extended [S3].
The House rule closed the bill to amendments and limited debate to one hour, so no floor changes were possible [S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: several billion dollars more per year for children's health coverage, financed mainly by tobacco taxes. The coverage gains are large and targeted at low-income families; the tax falls on consumers of a legal product with well-documented health costs. The main blemishes are the carve-out for billion-dollar corporations on a single estimated-tax quarter and the cap that blocks coverage for children above 300% of poverty. On balance, the benefits to low-income children clearly outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it, but the President vetoed it and the House couldn't muster the two-thirds needed to override, so the bill died.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 265-142 on October 25, 2007, with 222 of 233 Democrats in favor and 43 of 200 Republicans [S9].
The Senate passed it without amendment 64-30 on November 1, 2007, with all 49 Democrats, both independents, and 17 of 49 Republicans in favor [S12].
President Bush vetoed the bill on December 12, 2007, and the Chair laid his veto message before the House [S7].
The House voted to postpone consideration of the veto message until January 23, 2008, 211-180, with every Republican voting no [S13].
On January 23, 2008, the House sustained the veto: the override vote reached only 260-152, short of the two-thirds required, with 218 Democrats and 42 Republicans in favor [S15].
After the failed override, the House agreed without objection to refer the bill and veto message to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, where it ended [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies avoided the higher excise taxes that would have funded the expansion, and the President's position held. Low-income children went without the expanded coverage this bill would have provided; Congress later passed a similar reauthorization in the next Congress.

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Children's Health Insurance Program Reauthorization Act of 2007 and guided it through House passage.

for.name: 222 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage, 222-1, and later 218-1 on the override attempt.

for.name: 45 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously for cloture and for final Senate passage.

for.name: 17 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on Senate passage and on the cloture motion to proceed.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill on December 12, 2007, and sent his objections to the House.

against.name: 151 of 199 House Republicans
against.role: House Republicans who sustained the veto
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the override vote, keeping it short of the required two-thirds.

against.name: 141 of 200 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage; 164 also voted for the Barton motion to recommit with instructions to amend the bill.

against.name: Rep. Joe Barton
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to committee with instructions to report it back with amendments; the motion failed 164-242.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats were nearly unanimous in favor (222-1 in the House, 45-0 in the Senate), while most Republicans opposed it (43-141 for passage in the House, 17-30 in the Senate), though a minority of Republicans crossed over each time.

industries.note: The bill raises excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, smokeless and pipe tobacco to finance children's coverage, and imposes a floor-stock tax by April 1, 2008. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against the public benefit the tax would fund.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: Expanded CHIP enrollment brings more children into plans, including managed care entities that contract with state CHIP programs, and the bill extends Medicaid managed care quality safeguards to CHIP. Premium assistance options also route subsidies to employer-sponsored private coverage.

industries.industry: Federally qualified health centers and rural clinics
industries.note: The bill applies the prospective payment system to services they provide and more covered children means more reimbursed care.

industries.industry: Corporations with $1 billion or more in assets
industries.note: The bill trims their third-quarter 2012 estimated tax payment from 114.75% to 113.75% of the amount otherwise due — a modest, unadvertised benefit tucked into the revenue title.
